title: It's more than a competition – DVLA's Code Challenge

content.content: Every year at the DVLA Code Challenge final, people ask me the same question: "Which game is going to win?"

It's a fair question. The Code Challenge is a competition, and our finalists work incredibly hard to reach the final. But what excites me most is not who takes home the trophy. It’s seeing young people discover what they can achieve through coding.
For me, the real success of the Code Challenge is the confidence learners gain when they realise they can solve problems, bring ideas to life and create something they are proud of.
This year, 20 schools from across Wales submitted 54 games using Scratch, a beginner-friendly programming platform that helps young people learn coding through creativity and experimentation.
More than coding

The work starts long before pupils arrive at the Richard Ley Development Centre for the final. Throughout the year, participants develop ideas, test solutions and create games based on themes designed with our partner organisations. These themes encourage pupils to engage with real-world challenges and think about how technology can be used to address them.

Watching the finalists showcase their games, I was struck by their imagination, ambition and determination. The quality of the entries was impressive, but what stood out most was everything that happened behind the scenes.

Creating a game involves much more than learning how to code. Pupils work together, think logically, break down complex problems and find creative solutions. They learn how to test and improve their work, overcome setbacks and adapt their ideas when things do not go to plan.

For many participants, presenting to an audience can be just as challenging as building the game itself. Explaining how their game works, the decisions they made and the problems they solve helps them develop confidence and communication skills that extend far beyond the classroom.
Inspiring future opportunities
One of the most rewarding parts of the day was seeing pupils interact with professionals from public services, emergency services, technology and industry.

These conversations give participants a chance to learn more about different career paths and understand how digital skills are used in the workplace. For some, it is the first time they have spoken to people working in these fields. It can open their eyes to opportunities they may have never considered before.

The event is only possible because of the support we receive from teachers, STEM Ambassadors and our partner organisations. Their time, expertise and encouragement help create an environment where young people can learn, explore and grow in confidence.

This year’s event was supported by organisations including the Ministry of Defence, British Army, Mid and West Wales Fire and Rescue Service, STEM Wales, Swansea Council, British Computer Society, South Wales Police, Tarian ROCU, Road Safety Wales, Wild Connect, Free School Clothes, Welsh Stars and Buffoon Media.
Looking beyond the results

Of course, the competition element remains an important part of the day. This year’s winners, Parkland Primary School and Ysgol Gymraeg Ystalyfera Bro Dur, created engaging games that stood out in the final. Outstanding performances also came from Blaenbaglan Primary School, Hawarden Village Church School, Gowerton Comprehensive School and Rougemont School.
What I will remember most about this year's event is seeing pupils proudly explain their ideas, showcase their creativity and discover what they can achieve.

The Code Challenge teaches coding, but it also helps young people develop teamwork, communication, creativity and problem-solving skills. Whatever career they choose, those skills will stay with them throughout their lives.
That’s why the Code Challenge has always been about much more than competition.

description: DVLA's annual Code Challenge gives young people the opportunity to develop coding, creativity and problem-solving skills. John St C Williams reflects on this year's event and explains why its success is measured by much more than the final results.

title: A complex picture, but a clearer path: what the 2025 water classifications tell us about England’s waterways

content.content: Each time we publish the latest assessment of England's waters through the Water Environment (Water Framework Directive) Regulation classification, a familiar headline emerges: only a minority of rivers, lakes and estuaries achieve "good" overall status. It's a figure that invites a simple reading: that progress is “too slow”, that investment “hasn't delivered”, that the water environment is stagnating or declining. Those concerns are understandable, but they are not the full story.

The 2025 classifications give us a detailed picture of England's water environment and are a powerful indicator of where action is needed most. The headline result is that 14.3% of waterbodies are classified as at Good Ecological Status. To understand what that means, you need to dive below the headlines and understand how the system works.
One out, all out

The classification framework is deliberately demanding. The "one out, all out" approach we take means the overall status of a water body is determined by its lowest-scoring element. Every single element must pass for a water body to be classified as good. That ensures we do not overlook problems that matter to ecosystems - but it also means that progress can be real and measurable without being fully reflected in the headline figure. Around a third of water bodies that failed to achieve good status this time did so because of just one element. So these headline results provide a foundation for action, but they do not tell the whole story.
Beyond the headline figures

Beneath the headline, some parts of the picture are more encouraging. The underlying data shows 82% of individual ecological indicators are now classed  as Good or High status, demonstrating some underlying aspects of the health of many waterways are positive, even where overall classifications haven't shifted.  Ammonia - historically one of the most significant pressures on freshwater life - is at 92.9% good status, pointing to real, sustained progress in some areas.

There are, however, known pressures that cannot be resolved quickly. All surface waters continue to fail in chemical status, which reflects the presence of persistent legacy substances such as  brominated flame retardants, mercury and PFOS that will take decades to deplete.
Comparing to previous assessments

Some will remember that the figure reported in 2019 was 16.3%. It is tempting to read the difference as a decline, but the two datasets are not directly comparable. Assessment methods, monitoring and available evidence have all advanced. We have automated the assessment of Heavily Modified Water Bodies, updated baselines and removed historic "expert judgement" classifications, which increases transparency but reduces comparability with earlier cycles.

None of this reflects a weakening of the system, but a more rigorous and consistent one, meaning a water body can be classified at a lower status today not because its condition has worsened, but because we now understand it better. Read more about these changes on our Water Data Explorer | Engage Environment Agency
Better science, harder headlines

More work is needed to determine the causes of the results, but climate change, historic underinvestment, and improved monitoring are all likely factors. Stronger monitoring reveals issues that were previously hidden, giving us a firmer basis for decision-making, even where the picture looks tougher in the short term.

This is not a challenge England faces alone. Last year the European Environment Agency reported that picture across Europe remains very challenging, with a number of areas reporting below 10% Good Ecological Status by the latest 2021 statistics.
What happens next

So, what happens next? The classifications are a rigorous dataset that will drive evidence-led action through River Basin Management Plans (to be published over the winter), where communities, farmers and water companies work together to make improvements. These plans are majority funded by water companies, and the latest funding round saw £22.1 billion allocated to water environment improvements by 2030. The government's Water White Paper and the Environment Agency's EA2030 strategy reinforces this direction, with a stronger emphasis on data, partnerships and environmental outcomes.

That investment is already being put to work. It is funding the upgrade of 2,350 storm overflows, which is expected to reduce sewage spills by an estimated 85,000 a year. It is reducing phosphorus inputs to the environment at more than 800 sewage treatment works. And it is reducing the amount of water abstracted from rivers and groundwater, retaining an estimated 60 million litres of water in the environment every day. These are not abstract commitments: they are specific, measurable interventions that will show up in future classifications.

This is not just theory. The River Roch in Greater Manchester shows what classification-driven action looks like in practice: phosphate levels, which can harm river wildlife, have improved from poor in 2019 to good in 2025. Investigation traced earlier deterioration downstream to water company assets, leading to a catchment permit covering a whole group of sewage treatment works upstream of the Manchester Ship Canal, several of which were required to remove phosphate from their discharge for the first time. The result has been cleaner water, with the Ship Canal's deterioration reversed and further improvements in connected rivers, an example of how targeted action based on solid evidence delivers real results.

But we should be honest: investment takes time, and the environment takes longer to recover. We know the public want things to move faster, and progress won't always be visible in a single headline metric. That is how the 2025 classifications should be understood: not as a verdict on success or failure, but as a tool for improvement, showing us where the problems are, helping us target effort, and giving us the evidence to hold ourselves and others to account.
Turning evidence into action

Improving our waters depends on all of us working together - regulators, policymakers, water companies, land managers, communities and citizen scientists, at both local and national levels. We now have a clearer path than ever before.

These results should be seen as a starting point, not an end point. They give a clearer shared evidence base for understanding the condition of England’s waters, where pressures are greatest and where action can have most impact. Improving the water environment will be a long-term community journey, requiring the Environment Agency, government, water companies, farmers, businesses, local partners and the public to each play their part.

We will now working hard at local level to understand the complex causes behind why each waterbody gets a certain classification, so that we can plan investment and interventions over the next planning cycles.  We will keep refining how, where and what we monitor so that we can develop an ever more rigorous understanding of what interventions have the greatest impact.

Better evidence is only useful if matched by the ability to act. We have significantly increased our capacity to tackle water pollution, with more staff, better data and stronger powers. Last year we completed over 10,000 inspections of water company assets, and we plan to increase farm inspections to 6,000 a year over the next three years. Since 2015 we have concluded more than 70 prosecutions against water and sewerage companies, securing fines of over £158 million, and the Water (Special Measures) Act means we are better equipped than ever to drive the improvements the public rightly expect.
The task ahead is to follow the evidence together and turn shared evidence into real, lasting improvement for England's water environment.

title: Explore More for Less: Affordable East Midlands Nature Days Out

content.content: This summer, if you’re looking for fun and accessible days out that are low-cost, then we have you covered. Not only is spending time in nature great for your wellbeing, it can also be great for your bank balance. Here are our suggestions for our favourite affordable days out in the East Midlands!

The school holidays are here, and the East Midlands has some special places to explore - many of them free or very nearly so. Whether you're after a coastal walk, ancient woodland, or a magical trail through the forest, there's something for every family this summer. Here are five of our favourite affordable days out in nature across the East Midlands.
Lincolnshire Coronation Coast National Nature Reserve

Stretching for almost 30 kilometres along the Greater Lincolnshire coast, the Lincolnshire Coronation Coast National Nature Reserve (NNR), the first in the King’s Series of NNRs, is free to visit. The reserve brings together sand dunes, saltmarsh, mudflats and freshwater marshes of international importance, and is home to natterjack toads, grey seals, and a spectacular array of birds.

The reserve also forms part of the King Charles III England Coast Path (KCIIIECP), so you can combine a walk along one of England's great national trails with a chance to experience some truly special wildlife habitat. Cleethorpes and Mablethorpe neighbour the reserve, making it easily accessible and with plenty of options to grab some fish and chips before you head home!

Getting there: The reserve is accessible from several points along the Lincolnshire coast. Cleethorpes has a train station with regular services from Lincoln and Doncaster. Mablethorpe is accessible by bus from Lincoln.
Clumber Park, Nottinghamshire (National Trust)

Nestled in the ancient forest of Sherwood, Clumber Park is a picturesque 3,800-acre expanse of parkland, heath, woodland and lake that was once the country estate of the Dukes of Newcastle. This summer, it's easier than ever to get there without a car, and cheaper too.

A new daily bus service links Worksop Train Station, Worksop Bus Station and Clumber Park, running every day from 25 July to 6 September 2026. Return tickets cost just £3 per person and include free admission to the park.
National Trust members, under-fives, and visitors arriving at Worksop by train with a valid rail ticket all travel free and enter the park at no charge. Under 16s are free from 1 to 31 August.

Once you're there, the National Trust’s Summer of Play programme offers six interactive play zones, free ukulele workshops, storytelling sessions and much more, all included with entry. This year also sees Clumber take part in a nationwide National Trust partnership with Pokémon, meaning there’s enough entertainment for children of all ages.

Getting there: Bus service operates from Worksop Train Station (served by trains from Nottingham and Sheffield). Return bus ticket (£3) includes park entry. Service runs daily 25 July – 6 September 2026.
Bradgate Park and Swithland Wood National Nature Reserve, Leicestershire

Just a short journey from Leicester city centre, Bradgate Park is one of the region's most loved wild spaces. Spanning 438 hectares of rugged, ancient landscape, the park features ancient oak trees, roaming deer and some of the very oldest and rarest rocks on earth. The lower part of the park is accessible via a tarmac carriageway suitable for wheelchairs and pushchairs, and the visitor centre tells the story of the estate's fascinating natural and human history. Both the park and the visitor centre are free to enter.

This summer, families can also take part in the Moths and Butterflies Trail, running until 23 August 2026. Follow the path from Newtown Linford to the visitor centre, spot painted examples of the moths and butterflies found at Bradgate and Swithland Wood, collect hidden letters and solve the mystery moth, then claim your sticker prize at the visitor centre. It's a lovely free activity for children of all ages.

Getting there: Newtown Linford is served by bus from Leicester city centre (Arriva service 120 from St Margaret's Bus Station). The park entrance at Newtown Linford is a short walk from the bus stop. Bradgate Park also has three car parks, charges apply.
Forestry England Sherwood Pines, Nottinghamshire

Take a stroll into the deep dark wood for a day of adventure at Sherwood Pines. The forest is free to enter, with something for everyone: three waymarked walking trails, cycling trails for all abilities, and play areas throughout the woodland.

Families with young children will love the Gruffalo sculptures dotted through the trees and the Room on the Broom interactive trail, where children can help Witch find her lost hat, bow and wand while exploring the forest. Room on the Broom trail packs are available from the visitor centre for £4.

Getting there: Sherwood Pines is near Edwinstowe, Nottinghamshire. The nearest train station is Mansfield (Robin Hood Line from Nottingham), with onward bus connections via the number 14 or 15 bus from Mansfield bus station (next to the train station). If driving, car park charges apply to non-members.
The Pennine Bridleway, Derbyshire

For an accessible taste of Peak District scenery, head to Middleton Top, the southernmost start point of the Pennine Bridleway. This family-friendly, mostly flat trail follows the route of the old Cromford and High Peak Railway, and is suitable for walking, cycling or wheeling, making it a great option for families with pushchairs or wheelchair users. There's a visitor centre, café and toilets on site, plus a picnic area at the adjacent Redhill Quarry Nature Reserve. The historic Engine House is open some weekends (fees apply).

Alternatively, further along the route, the picturesque village of Hayfield offers access to a short, one-mile stretch of the Sett Valley Trail, also following a former railway line through wildlife-rich woodland. The trail runs alongside the village bus station, with a handful of cafes, pubs and shops, plus a picnic area and toilets nearby.

If you'd rather see more of the Peak District without the walk, the Stagecoach Peak Sightseer open-top bus is worth considering. Running daily until 19 September, it offers hop-on, hop-off travel between destinations including Chatsworth, Bakewell, Castleton and Hathersage, so you can enjoy the views and dip into a village or two without lacing up your walking boots. It isn't a free option (a family day ticket costs £38), but it's a flexible way to see a lot of the National Park in a single day.

Getting there: Middleton Top is on local bus routes, with connections from Cromford, Matlock and Matlock Bath train stations. Hayfield's Sett Valley Trail runs alongside Hayfield bus station. The Peak Sightseer can be joined at various stops including Chatsworth and Bakewell. There are also morning journeys from Chesterfield train station and South Sheffield to Chatsworth with return journeys late afternoon.
A few more favourites

Of course, this is not an exhaustive list and there are so many more great places to get out in nature on our doorstep that we couldn’t possibly name them all. Here are a few more though which are family friendly and free to enter:

Or for some options even closer to home Local Nature Reserves are places valued for their wildlife or geology, designated by local councils for people to enjoy and learn from. Find your nearest one: Local Nature Reserves (England) | Natural England Open Data Geoportal

With the recent dry, hot weather, wildfire risk is high across the countryside. Please pack a picnic instead of a barbecue, take your rubbish home with you, and if you spot an unattended fire, get to a safe place and call 999.
Remember to always follow the Countryside Code when you’re out and about in nature!

The Countryside Code is a simple guide to helping everyone enjoy the outdoors responsibly while protecting the natural environment. It encourages visitors to respect other people, protect plants, animals and habitats, and leave gates, paths and property as they find them. By following the Countryside Code, we can all play our part in keeping nature accessible, safe and enjoyable for everyone, while helping to conserve the landscapes and wildlife that make our countryside so special.

title: Apply for the Farmer Welfare Grant

content.content: Applications for the new and expanded Farmer Welfare Grant are now open.

The grant will provide £1.5 million over 3 years to support projects for both the personal and business resilience of farmers that strengthen the mental health, wellbeing, and resilience of farming communities across England.

Farming is at the heart of our food system and rural economy, but we know that many farmers face significant challenges. Long hours, isolation, financial pressures, unpredictable weather and the demands of running a business can all affect wellbeing.
The Farmer Welfare Grant will fund organisations that are already working closely with farming communities, enabling them to deliver targeted support where it is needed most.
Building on the success of the previous Farmer Welfare Grant, this expanded funding will support practical interventions that will continue to deliver benefits into the future.
Apply now
The application portal is open from 6 August until midday on 9 September.
Before applying, we encourage all applicants to read the guidance carefully and review the eligibility criteria.
You can ask clarification questions in the application portal until 28 August. All questions and answers will be public to keep access to information fair and open.
Applicants needing support with the application portal can raise a support ticket or contact the portal help desk between 08:00-18:00 Monday - Friday (excluding Bank Holidays) on 029 2279 0054.
You can learn more about navigating the portal in one of our webinars, mentioned below.
Notification of outcomes
Once the application window has closed, the applications will be reviewed and scored by a panel of policy and delivery experts from Defra.
Funding decisions will be made after all applications have been assessed. We expect all applicants will be notified of the outcome in October.

If you're considering applying, our webinars will provide further information about the grant and application process.

title: We're Building the Future of User-Centred Design at HMCTS
authors: Rachel Callear, Head of User-Centred Design, User Experience and Insight

content.content: [English] - [Cymraeg]

Earlier this month, I shared how we're strengthening user-centred design (UCD) at HMCTS and why investing in design capability is so important to improving justice services. If you haven't read that blog yet, I'd encourage you to start there.
In this blog, I want to focus on what's next. Simply put, we're building something exciting and we're looking for talented people to help shape it.
A unique opportunity to join us at a pivotal moment

We've set out a clear ambition for the future of UCD at HMCTS. We're creating a stronger in-house profession, growing our expertise and ensuring user needs are at the centre of how we design and improve services.

That means we're expanding our team and recruiting more permanent civil servants across the UCD function, including 6 senior leaders across interaction and content design who will champion their professions and work alongside service design and user research to embed iterative user-centred design approaches across HMCTS.

This is more than a recruitment campaign, it's an opportunity to join a profession that is growing, influencing decisions and helping shape services used by millions of people, from members of the public and legal professionals to court and tribunal staff.

You'll be joining at a time when the function is evolving. You'll have the opportunity not just to contribute to services, but to help shape the future direction of UCD within one of the largest organisations in government.
Work that really matters
Designing for justice is different.

Our users are often navigating situations that can be stressful, unfamiliar and life-changing. They may be resolving family disputes, attending court, seeking compensation, appealing decisions or progressing a case through the justice system. Good design can make those experiences clearer, simpler and less daunting. That makes the work both challenging and rewarding.

Our teams tackle complex problems every day, working across organisational boundaries, balancing user needs with operational realities and designing services that work for a wide range of users. For UCD professionals who want to make a meaningful impact, there aren't many opportunities quite like it.
Building a multidisciplinary community

We're investing in all areas of user-centred design, including service design, content design and interaction design. We've already made great progress in growing the profession, but we're not standing still.

We’re continuing to strengthen our content and interaction design capability as we build a more balanced and mature multidisciplinary function. We know that excellent digital services rely on strong design expertise, and we're keen to attract people who are passionate about creating intuitive, accessible and user-focused experiences.

Alongside recruitment, we're building a strong professional community where people can develop their skills, share knowledge and learn from one another. We want HMCTS to be a place where UCD professionals can build long-term careers and do some of the best work of their lives.
Strengthening our interaction and content design capabilities

Our interaction designers work across internal and public-facing services, creating accessible, inclusive experiences that put user needs first. Working closely with researchers, accessibility specialists, content designers and developers, they use a range of techniques to test and refine ideas, from early sketches to coded prototypes. The team also shares learning across government and has recently explored how AI could enhance both the way we work and the services we deliver.

Our content designers work across GOV.UK guidance and digital services, ensuring users get the right information at the right point in their journey. By working across both areas, designers build broad expertise, share knowledge and support one another to continually improve the quality and consistency of our content.

Both professions play a vital role in helping us design services that are simple, accessible and centred around user needs. As our teams grow, we are focusing on working more strategically, strengthening collaboration across HMCTS and making the most of new technologies, including AI, to improve outcomes for users.
To support this, we'll soon introduce a new multidisciplinary team model, enabling senior designers to act as UCD leads and provide stronger user-centred leadership across services.
Why join HMCTS?
People often join HMCTS because they want to work on services that matter.
They stay because of the scale of the challenges, the opportunity to influence change and the supportive community around them.
Our teams work with researchers, developers, product managers, operational colleagues and policy experts to solve real problems for real users.

You'll have the opportunity to work across a broad and varied portfolio of services, develop your professional skills and contribute to work with a direct impact on access to justice. Most importantly, you'll be part of a community that cares deeply about improving outcomes for users.
Come and help us build what's next
We're proud of what we've achieved so far, but we know there's much more to do.

As we continue to grow our UCD profession, we're looking for talented people who are curious, collaborative and passionate about creating better services. If that sounds like you, we'd love to hear from you.
Keep an eye on Civil Service Jobs and HMCTS recruitment channel for upcoming opportunities. The future of user-centred design at HMCTS is being built right now. We'd love you to be part of it.

Rydym yn parhau i gryfhau ein gallu dylunio cynnwys a rhyngweithio wrth i ni adeiladu swyddogaeth amlddisgyblaethol fwy cytbwys ac aeddfed. Rydym yn gwybod bod gwasanaethau digidol rhagorol yn dibynnu ar arbenigedd dylunio cryf, ac rydym yn awyddus i ddenu pobl sy'n angerddol am greu profiadau greddfol, hygyrch a chanolbwyntio ar y defnyddiwr.

Ochr yn ochr â recriwtio, rydym yn adeiladu cymuned broffesiynol gref lle gall pobl ddatblygu eu sgiliau, rhannu gwybodaeth a dysgu oddi wrth ei gilydd. Rydym am i GLlTEF fod yn lle, lle gall gweithwyr proffesiynol UCD adeiladu gyrfaoedd hirdymor a gwneud rhai o waith gorau eu bywydau.
Cryfhau ein galluoedd dylunio rhyngweithio a chynnwys

Mae ein dylunwyr rhyngweithio yn gweithio ar draws gwasanaethau mewnol a chyhoeddus, gan greu profiadau hygyrch, cynhwysol sy'n rhoi anghenion defnyddwyr yn gyntaf. Gan weithio'n agos gydag ymchwilwyr, arbenigwyr hygyrchedd, dylunwyr cynnwys a datblygwyr, maent yn defnyddio ystod o dechnegau i brofi a mireinio syniadau, o frasluniau cynnar i brototeipiau wedi'u codio. Mae'r tîm hefyd yn rhannu dysgu ar draws y llywodraeth ac yn ddiweddar mae wedi archwilio sut y gallai AI wella'r ffordd rydym yn gweithio a'r gwasanaethau rydym yn eu darparu.

Mae ein dylunwyr cynnwys yn gweithio ar draws canllawiau GOV.UK a gwasanaethau digidol, gan sicrhau bod defnyddwyr yn cael yr wybodaeth gywir ar y pwynt iawn yn eu taith. Trwy weithio ar draws y ddau faes, mae dylunwyr yn adeiladu arbenigedd eang, yn rhannu gwybodaeth ac yn cefnogi ei gilydd i wella ansawdd a chysondeb ein cynnwys yn barhaus.

Mae'r ddau broffesiwn yn chwarae rhan hanfodol wrth ein helpu i ddylunio gwasanaethau sy'n syml, hygyrch ac sy'n canolbwyntio ar anghenion defnyddwyr. Wrth i'n timau dyfu, rydym yn canolbwyntio ar weithio'n fwy strategol, cryfhau cydweithredu ar draws GLlTEF a manteisio i'r eithaf ar dechnolegau newydd, gan gynnwys AI, i wella canlyniadau i ddefnyddwyr.

Er mwyn cefnogi hyn, byddwn yn cyflwyno model tîm amlddisgyblaethol newydd cyn bo hir, sy'n galluogi uwch ddylunwyr i weithredu fel arweinwyr UCD a darparu arweinyddiaeth gryfach sy'n canolbwyntio ar y defnyddiwr ar draws gwasanaethau.
Pam ymuno â GLlTEF?
Mae pobl yn aml yn ymuno â GLlTEF oherwydd eu bod eisiau gweithio ar wasanaethau sy'n bwysig.
Maen nhw'n aros oherwydd graddfa'r heriau, y cyfle i ddylanwadu ar newid a'r gymuned gefnogol o'u cwmpas.
Mae ein timau'n gweithio gydag ymchwilwyr, datblygwyr, rheolwyr cynnyrch, cydweithwyr gweithredol ac arbenigwyr polisi i ddatrys problemau go iawn i ddefnyddwyr go iawn.

Byddwch yn cael y cyfle i weithio ar draws portffolio eang ac amrywiol o wasanaethau, datblygu eich sgiliau proffesiynol a chyfrannu at weithio gydag effaith uniongyrchol ar fynediad at gyfiawnder. Yn bwysicaf oll, byddwch chi'n rhan o gymuned sy'n poeni'n ddwfn am wella canlyniadau i ddefnyddwyr.
Dewch i'n helpu i adeiladu'r hyn sydd nesaf
Rydyn ni'n falch o'r hyn rydyn ni wedi'i gyflawni hyd yn hyn, ond rydyn ni'n gwybod bod llawer mwy i'w wneud.

Wrth i ni barhau i dyfu ein proffesiwn UCD, rydym yn chwilio am bobl dalentog sy'n chwilfrydig, cydweithredol ac angerddol am greu gwasanaethau gwell. Os yw hynny'n swnio fel chi, byddem wrth ein bodd yn clywed gennych.

Cadwch lygad ar sianeli recriwtio Civil Service Jobs a GLlTEF am gyfleoedd sydd i ddod. Mae dyfodol dylunio sy'n canolbwyntio ar y defnyddiwr yn GLlTEF yn cael ei adeiladu ar hyn o bryd. Byddem wrth ein bodd i chi fod yn rhan ohono.

title: Family nutrition, farming and no fuss IP

content.content: For Milly Fyfe MBE, founder of her No Fuss Meals for Busy Parents community interest company (CIC), what began as a simple blog during the pandemic documenting family life on her farm and sharing her home-made recipes, quickly grew into something far bigger and meaningful.

With the addition of The Countryside Kitchen – an on-farm educational space for people of all ages and abilities – and a community shop, No Fuss Meals is now a thriving social enterprise, connecting people with food, farming and wellbeing.

We spoke to Milly about protecting the intellectual property (IP) in her business – safeguarding the brand identity and community infrastructure she’s worked so hard to build, as well as setting the foundations for the business’ future growth.
It’s all in the name
Milly explained how her understanding of intellectual property, and the importance of identifying and protecting these important assets, grew as her business expanded:
Milly has taken proactive steps to secure her brand through registered trade marks, including her personal name and company logo: Click here to view the 'No Fuss Meals For Busy Parents' trade mark

However, Milly admits she wasn't always so IP savvy. She worked with a trade mark attorney to register her personal name, then sought support from her local Business and IP Centre (BIPC) and the Intellectual Property Office (IPO), giving her the confidence to trade mark her business name herself.
You can learn more about the different types of trade marks and registration criteria here: Register a trade mark : What you can register as a trade mark - GOV.UK
Overcoming challenges

As with most businesses, the journey to success doesn't come without its hurdles. Milly recalls a time during the trade mark application process when a potential conflict was flagged with a similarly named company:
“One of your (IPO) colleagues rang me up and told me about a company with similar wording and asked if I still wanted to proceed. I thought ‘oh no’.”
Thankfully for Milly, further investigation revealed the other business was inactive, and no formal objection followed.
Milly praised the support she received from the IPO, in particular the checks and due diligence put in place to help applicants successfully navigate the process:

“When you're doing something new it does feel like you're going out in the dark, but there are lots of people there to help you along the way. It's not like you're spending money and just hoping for the best. You (IPO) are very supportive and helpful.”
The benefits of IP

Milly explained that whilst her trade marks haven't directly influenced any funding decisions, they have contributed to a broader picture of professionalism. For a growing social enterprise engaging with a variety of partners, she feels that credibility is invaluable:
As Milly’s personal profile grows through her media and presenting work, protecting her name and brand has become even more significant:
“In today’s society, especially with social media, it's very easy for others to jump on the back of something. Protecting your brand helps prevent that.”
Advice for other businesses
Reflecting on her business journey, we asked Milly what advice she would give to other businesses just starting out. Her message was clear, don't overlook intellectual property:

“It's something you should consider as you're setting up and then as you continue to grow, looking ahead to the future. If you don't, things can quickly be taken from you, so it’s important to protect what you're building”.
What's next?

Following the success of The Countryside Kitchen, (and well earned recognition in The Kings Birthday Honours with an MBE award for services to Farmers and Family Nutrition) Milly Fyfe has her sights set on an even bigger project: to influence future policy on healthy eating and improving access to farm education.

And of course, intellectual property will continue to play a key role at each stage of Milly's journey, protecting her business name and logo while she contributes to a movement rooted in food, community, and wellbeing.
Are you a small business looking for IP guidance? Take a look at our step by step guide to find out what IP might be right for you:Get intellectual property rights: step-by-step - GOV.UK

title: Shape the future: apply now for the Youth Climate and Nature Panel

content.content: The decisions we take now to address climate change and restore nature will define the country that today’s young people will inherit.
We want the next generation to inherit solutions, not challenges.

Today’s young people are already helping to develop solutions – in their schools, communities, workplaces and families and bring different experiences, fresh ideas and a clear understanding of what environmental change means for their communities and their futures. It is therefore essential that they have meaningful opportunities not simply to hear about government policy, but to help shape it.
That is why we are delighted that recruitment has opened for the government’s first Youth Climate and Nature Panel.
A new national panel
The panel was first announced by the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero in December 2025 as part of Energising Britain: Your voice in our Clean Energy Superpower Mission.

It will bring together 15 young people aged 16 to 25 from across the UK and from a wide range of backgrounds, experiences and perspectives. Panel members will share their views with government, provide insight and advice, strengthen engagement with other young people and help encourage collaboration between generations.

Importantly, the panel members will help determine their own priorities. This will give them the space to focus on the climate and nature issues they believe matter most and ensure their views and experiences help inform government thinking.

The issues they could consider range from how we are restoring nature, adapting for climate change, improving access to nature, and the quality of the environment, to how we are transitioning to clean energy, a sustainable food system, and a circular economy, underpinned by green jobs.
Bringing community voices into climate and nature policymaking

The new panel forms part of a wider commitment to involve  communities in climate and nature policymaking, as set out in our Energising Britain Plan and embedded in our Environmental Improvement Plan.
This means designing policy with people, rather than simply expecting them to respond once decisions have already been taken.

Youth perspectives will be increasingly important as government delivers ambitious programmes across climate and nature policy. These include efforts to protect 30% of land and sea for nature by 2030, support large-scale nature recovery, attract private investment into environmental improvement, and deliver the transition to clean energy and a net zero economy. Hearing directly from younger generations can help ensure these policies deliver benefits that are fair, practical and lasting.

Across Defra and its organisations, we are already learning from different approaches. Members of the public have helped inform the development of the government’s food strategy through a Citizen Advisory Council. At the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, its Youth Council works with senior leaders so that young people’s views are reflected in organisational decisions.
It could be you!
Applications are now open to young people aged 16 to 25 who are based anywhere in the UK.
We are particularly keen to hear from young people with different interests, experiences and relationships with climate, nature and the environment.

It could be someone interested in how farmers are helping restore nature, how renewable energy projects are shaping local areas, how towns and cities can become greener and more climate resilient, or how new green careers and technologies will affect the future economy

We also want to hear from young people who may never have joined an environmental group, attended a protest or spoken to government before. Personal experience, curiosity and a willingness to contribute are just as valuable as established knowledge of climate or nature policy.

Applicants do not need to be policy experts. What matters is that they are interested in sharing their perspective, listening to others and helping government understand how its decisions affect young people.
Applications close on Friday 11 September 2026.
Find out more and apply to join the Youth Climate and Nature Panel.
Hearing from younger voices
Alongside recruitment for the panel, the government has launched Young Voices for Climate and Nature.

This gives children and young people aged 16 and under the opportunity to share the climate and nature ideas that matter most to them through their school, community, sports, faith or other youth group.
Contributions can take many forms, including videos, artwork, letters, poems, essays, audio recordings and presentations. These ideas will help inform the panel’s work when it begins later this year.
The deadline for entries is Friday 23 October 2026.
Find out more about Young Voices for Climate and Nature and share your ideas.
Help us spread the word
Schools, colleges, charities, youth organisations, community groups and environmental networks all have an important role to play in helping this opportunity reach young people.
Please share details through your networks, membership groups, youth programmes and communications channels, and encourage the young people and youth groups you work with to apply or contribute.

Think particularly about young people whose voices may not usually be heard in national conversations about climate and nature, but whose everyday experiences could bring important insight to the panel.

By bringing a wider range of voices, experiences and ideas into government, we can develop better-informed policies and give young people a meaningful role in shaping the future of our climate and natural environment.

title: Prevent Programme Factsheet - August 2026

content.content: What is Prevent?

The UK has one of the most robust counter-terrorism frameworks in the world. Prevent is one of the four pillars of CONTEST, the UK’s counter-terrorism strategy. It operates in the non-criminal space and is designed to support people away from radicalisation before they commit an offence.

Prevent is underpinned by the Counter-Terrorism and Security Act 2015 (CTSA), which places a duty on public bodies, including schools, colleges, universities, health, local authorities, police, and prisons to prevent people from being drawn into terrorism. It operates across England, Wales, and Scotland.

Prevent deals with all forms of terrorism, including Islamist and Extreme Right-Wing ideologies, and emerging threats. As an early intervention programme, Prevent must consider susceptibility to involvement in terrorism, rather than be limited to cases where an ideology has already taken hold. Prevent is constantly evolving to reflect the changing threat and learning lessons from operational delivery to inform most effective management of risk. While Prevent cannot eliminate all risk, we aim to ensure that the Programme is robust, proportionate, and effective in protecting the public.
Key Themes from the Statistics
How Prevent Works

A Prevent referral is a safeguarding referral made to the police when there are concerns that a person may be susceptible to radicalisation or could be at risk of becoming involved in or supporting terrorism.
A Prevent referral does not lead to a criminal record, it is about safeguarding those that are at risk of radicalisation and protecting the public from harm and operates in the non-criminal space.
Those who are worried about someone at risk of becoming involved in, or supporting, terrorism, should share their concerns with the police.

To keep up with the pace of changing technology, the Home Office is testing new approaches to better spot and refer individuals at risk of radicalisation online, and how these insights can be translated into timely, proportionate interventions. This is particularly important considering the rise in children being arrested for terrorism related activity, much of which is carried out online.
Making a referral

If concerning behaviours are noticed, professionals should consider whether they indicate the person is at risk of becoming involved in, or supporting, terrorism. Professionals working in sectors covered by the statutory Prevent duty should follow the ‘notice, check, share’ process to determine if the concern is relevant to Prevent. This includes checking those concerns with the person responsible for safeguarding within their organisation, such as the designated safeguarding lead, and by referring to the Prevent duty training Awareness and Referrals courses.

If there remains a concern that someone is at risk of becoming involved in, or supporting, terrorism, the concern should be shared by making a referral to the police using the Prevent National Referral Form (NRF). The NRF helps professionals to articulate their concern and includes factors to consider as part of a referral.

Members of the public who are concerned that someone may be becoming radicalised should visit ACT Early for advice, support and information on making a Prevent referral or call the national police Prevent advice line on 0800 011 3764 to discuss their concerns.
What happens when a referral is made?

Once a referral is submitted, it is assessed by specialist police officers using the Prevent Assessment Framework (PAF). The PAF, when completed, provides an overview of a person’s susceptibility to radicalisation, and their risks of committing or supporting terrorism. It is used to underpin the decision on whether the referral should progress to a multi-agency panel, called Channel. Referrals deemed not suitable for Prevent may not require any further action, or may be signposted to alternative services for support, such as education or health.
What is Channel?

Channel is Prevent’s multi-agency safeguarding programme that provides early support to people who are assessed as being susceptible to radicalisation and at risk of being drawn into terrorism. Channel is voluntary and consent based.
Channel panels operate across England and Wales. In Scotland, the multi-agency panel is known as Prevent Multi-Agency Panel (PMAP).

The Channel panel is chaired by the local authority and can include a variety of partners such as the police, children’s services, social services, education professionals and mental health care professionals.
Referrals progressed to Channel will be considered by the panel, and where appropriate, the panel will decide on a tailored package of support that can be offered to the person.

In some cases, people who are already known to counter-terrorism partners may still benefit from early intervention support, which remains voluntary and consent based. Any decision to provide Channel support is carefully assessed, risk-managed and agreed with the relevant partners, beforehand.  Public safety remains the priority.
What kind of support is offered via Channel?

If a Channel intervention is required, a tailored support package will be offered. This could include mentoring, theological guidance, education, and careers assistance to those assessed as being at risk of radicalisation and requiring support.

Channel is voluntary and people who are referred to Prevent and assessed as at risk of radicalisation must give consent (via a parent or guardian if they are under 18) before they can be given support.

If a person does not engage with Channel or decides not to continue with the process for any reason, alternative forms of support may be available from the local authority or other providers. Any risks are then carefully managed by the police.

If there is an escalation of risk, where deemed appropriate, the police may transfer a case from Channel to a Police-Led Partnership (PLP). PLP covers the management of individuals that are not suitable for Channel, but which have identified Prevent-relevant issues requiring support or mitigation. PLPs are led by police but work in partnership with other agencies and employ many of the same type of approaches used within the multiagency processes of Channel.

title: The Prime Minister’s Commitment to Adult Social Care

content.content: Last week the Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, set out his commitment to reform adult social care and deliver a National Care Service.
Speaking at a care home in Golders Green on 29 July, he recognised that it requires fresh thinking and cross-party collaboration to make long-term reform possible.

Most of us have our own personal interaction with social care, either for ourselves or for family or friends. The Prime Minister talked about his – the excellent care shown to his father – and paid huge tribute to the care workforce and the work of great care organisations around the country. But he also recognised that there are fundamental issues to tackle, highlighting unacceptable levels of unmet need, the high costs of care and the importance of more support for the social care workforce.

Key to reforming the adult social care system will be the findings of the Independent Commission led by Baroness Louise Casey, which was set up last year to look at both shorter-term improvements to the social care system and the bigger questions that will lead us to a National Care Service. The Prime Minister announced that the Commission’s work will now be accelerated, delivering its report by summer 2027. The Prime Minister also announced that he will hold cross party talks with the leaders of the Liberal Democrat and Conservative parties.

The Prime Minister also made clear that the government will not wait until next summer to continue improving the social care system. He and the Secretary of State for Health, Yvette Cooper, talked about a new group bringing together all relevant ministers from across government, including the Chancellor and the Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government, to drive progress. This will include looking at ways to broaden the Fair Pay Agreement into a bigger reform to bring the workforce closer to NHS standards in terms of pay and progression routes; and ensuring tangible progress is made on the recommendations Baroness Casey has made already on improving support for those with dementia and motor neurone disease and strengthening adult safeguarding.
The Big Conversation on Care

Baroness Casey also launched the ‘Big Conversation on Care’ last week, running until April 2027. This extensive engagement exercise presents a major opportunity for people with lived experience, families, carers and the wider public, to give their views on the future of adult social care and the big questions that underpin its reform.

While Baroness Casey’s work is independent of government, I would urge you all to get involved with The Big Conversation on Care and to share this opportunity to steer the future of adult social care in this country with your networks – professionally and personally. You can find more information on the ‘The Big Conversation on Care’ at the Commission’s website.

title: GDS: delivering a better GOV.UK experience for business

content.content: GDS and BIST (Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade) are taking action to deliver government’s ambitions to drive growth into every postcode, reduce the costs of doing business and create a more productive and agile environment. Helping more businesses find the support and services available more quickly will unlock innovation, encourage investment and enable them to flourish.

The government is already overhauling the regulatory landscape to reduce complexity and duplication. BIST recently published a Regulation Action Plan Progress Report, committing to reducing administrative burdens on business by 25% (£5.6bn) by the end of parliament.

GDS and BIST are also partnering to deliver on commitments made in A blueprint for modern digital government to help businesses start and scale – delivering government services that work for businesses as well as they do for citizens.
The challenges businesses face

There are continuing efforts to make things simpler on GOV.UK. Government offers a wealth of resources and information to benefit businesses, but we see potential to make it simpler for people to find what they need.

The State of digtial government review found that because information is often shared across different government services, this can lead to duplication. For example, to start a business today, people need to:

To achieve this, people have to find and look at multiple pieces of advice spread across numerous government organisations and website pages, using more than one logged-in account. We want to streamline this. GDS and BIST’s joint research has identified at least 160 services related to business, demonstrating just how complex the system can sometimes feel for people.
Creating a better experience

A more consistent way to access government services will help to make the experience more efficient, reduce the risk of duplication and help to counter fraudulent behaviour. To achieve this, we’re going to provide a single, proactive and personalised experience for business through GOV.UK and its channels, capabilities and components.

This will ensure that businesses only have one place to transact with government, including knowing where to start and what to do next, finding funding opportunities and getting access to people, expertise or professional networks.

We already know that when businesses access support it has a positive impact on growth, but information is often split across several different digital services or isn’t specific enough to meet people’s needs.
What we’re improving
To ensure we make progress quickly, a new team has been set up in GDS to lead the delivery of improved businesses interactions with government online.

Building on discovery and testing to date, the team will undertake extensive research with business users and translate their findings into deliverable products and services, designed with and for businesses.

Bringing together BIST’s strong relationships with HMRC, Companies House and business, as well as harnessing GDS’s expertise in digital transformation, the team will also be able to support early identification and delivery of priority improvements for GOV.UK.
How we’ll test and learn

It’s our intention to build a unified GOV.UK experience for business through phased delivery rather than a ‘big bang’ release, and we’ll co-design any solutions we put in place with businesses and government.

We want everything we develop and implement to add value and, over time, take us closer to a full-service offering. We’ll be looking for quick wins too, like GOV.UK content improvements that will form the foundations for a better offer overall.

We’ll also be collaborating with stakeholders to shape our plans, scope and priorities. So far, they have told us they’d like to see links to BIST’s own Smart Data agenda, fraud prevention and how we could benchmark against other international governments working in the same problem space.

You’ll hear more from the team soon about our roadmap for delivery and opportunities to engage. Until then, what other issues do you think we need to address? We’d love to hear more from by email: gdsbusiness@dsit.gov.uk

title: Minutes published of UK NSC June 2026 meeting

content.content: The UK National Screening Committee (UK NSC) has published the minutes of its June 2026 meeting.
Topics discussed by committee members at the meeting included:

Committee members agreed that newborn screening for CMV should not be recommended because there is not enough evidence to show screening would offer clear benefits compared to existing clinical management. However, they asked for more in-depth work to be commissioned on antenatal screening for CMV after hearing that some blood tests in early pregnancy might help identify women with primary CMV infection, which can sometimes lead to serious harm for the baby.
The UK NSC also decided that more work, including engagement with relevant clinical experts, should be carried out into placenta function screening to reduce the risk of stillbirth.

The UK NSC maintained its recommendation against screening for IDA in pregnancy. The committee recognises IDA as an important health condition, but members agreed that the amount and type of international scientific studies are not robust enough to make a positive screening recommendation. So no further evidence work will be commissioned at this time.

Members reiterated their recommendation against screening for antenatal and postnatal mental health conditions. A screening programme cannot work without a good predictive test. Although there was a large volume of evidence, the evidence for individual tests was limited and what evidence there was suggested that the ability of tests to predict illness was not good.

The UK NSC also maintained its recommendation against population screening for COPD. An evidence map found no robust evidence that screening would improve illness, reduce deaths or improve health-related quality of life. As this topic has been examined before with the same conclusion, members decided it should no longer be routinely reviewed and would therefore be archived. Stakeholders can submit an open call proposal for the UK NSC to reopen this topic if new evidence becomes available that is likely to have a significant impact on the recommendation.

A proposal for targeted screening for pancreatic cancer was submitted through the 2024 open call for topics and the UK NSC commissioned an evidence map on targeted screening of people at high risk of the condition. The evidence was limited and the study designs susceptible to bias, which may lead to an inaccurate understanding of its use in screening. The committee decided no further evidence review work should be carried out at this time and any future requests to examine this topic should be made through the open call process.

Chair’s action was taken to maintain the UK NSC’s position not to recommend newborn screening for biliary atresia due to a lack of evidence on test accuracy or improved outcomes following screening. This topic will remain on the UK NSC’s regular review list.
Keep up to date

The UK NSC blog provides up to date news from the UK NSC. You can register to receive updates direct to your inbox, so there is no need to keep checking for new articles. If you have any questions about this blog article, or about the work of the UK NSC, please email uknsc@dhsc.gov.uk.

title: Update on the National Adult Safeguarding Board – Social work with adults

content.content: On 25th June, I updated on the first meeting of the National Adults Safeguarding Board (NASB) that is now established in direct response to Baroness Casey's initial recommendations on safeguarding.

I have received lots of questions about the Board and it is hugely encouraging to see how much interest there is in adult safeguarding and opportunity the new Board creates to have impact on reducing the risks of abuse and neglect to adults who may have care and support needs.

Reflecting on the last 10 years or more since the Care Act was introduced, there is no doubt that experience, expertise and understanding of adult safeguarding has grown considerably. I strongly welcome Baroness Casey's recommendation to review the legislative framework for adult safeguarding. The Board agreed to scope this review, to get on with reviewing the existing statutory guidance and to improve how data can be used at local and national levels.

In March 2026, we established a safeguarding Challenge Group with sector experts to review the Government response to individual Safeguarding Adults Reviews (SARs) that are escalated through the National Safeguarding Adults Boards Chairs network. There were several escalations that required a national response, and I am pleased to say that working together the Challenge Group have now agreed proposed actions on all escalated SARs.

As well as recommendations for national action, the escalation protocol allows local Safeguarding Boards to escalate SARs where there is learning to share nationally. The NASB has a role in ensuring learning is shared and action is embedded in local systems, so I strongly encourage local Boards to escalate SARs that have national learning.

The NASB will need to iterate over the next 12 months as it develops ways to strengthen national accountability and support local practice improvement. This will include evolving membership and strengthening co-production to ensure people-shaped design.

There is a commitment to openness and transparency and to this end we have set up a new page on gov.uk to keep you informed of progress National Adult Safeguarding Board - GOV.UK. This page will contain more detail about Board meetings as they happen, what was discussed and agreed actions. As priorities evolve, it is intended this page will become a repository for the reports on the data and themes we gather and action being taken.
The Board will meet quarterly, and the next meeting will take place on 5 October 2026.

title: How we used AI to help government manage its email backlog

content.content: Imagine inheriting a filing cabinet. Not a neat, organised one, but a vast, overflowing one that has been added to for fifteen years by dozens of different people, never sorted, never labelled, and now legally yours to manage. You need to know what's in it, what to keep, what to delete and what might be sensitive. And there are thousands more like it across the building. That is not far from the reality facing Knowledge and Information Management (KIM) professionals working with government email today. The problem hiding in plain sight Email is everywhere in government, and it has been accumulating for decades. Unlike documents stored in formal systems, email tends to pile up quietly. It’s a mixture of business decisions, administrative threads, sensitive exchanges and personal messages, all sitting together with no obvious way to tell them apart. At some point, someone must go through it. That someone is usually a KIM specialist, and the process is painstaking. Mailbox by mailbox, email by email, they work through content that can run into the hundreds of thousands of items. They need to make judgements about what is worth keeping for the long term and what meets legal and compliance requirements. They also assess what might be sensitive enough to need careful handling, including decisions about whether it can be shared or released at all. It is skilled, important work and at the scale government operates, doing it manually simply is not sustainable. This is the problem Project Kestrel was built to explore. Led by the AI Data Readiness Incubator team within Government Digital Service and developed in close collaboration with the Government KIM team, Phase 1 set out to test whether modern data science techniques could offer a better way. Not to replace human judgement, but to support it, making the work faster, more consistent and easier to explain. The data problem behind the data problem Here is where it gets interesting. Before the team could even begin testing new approaches to email management, they ran into a challenge that will feel familiar to anyone working on data innovation in government: you cannot safely experiment with the data you need. Real government emails contain personal information, sensitive material and content that is legally protected. Using them to develop and test new tools, however well-intentioned, creates real risks. So, the team made a deliberate choice, rather than finding ways to work around that constraint, they would solve it directly. The result is Tiger Heron, a synthetic email generator. Using large language models, Tiger Heron produces realistic-looking emails that closely resemble the kind of content government teams encounter in practice, without containing any real or sensitive information. Teams can build with it, test with it, break things with it and start again, all without ever touching a real inbox. This might sound like a workaround, but it is something more significant than that. Access to a safe, realistic data set is one of the most common blockers to data innovation in the public sector. Tiger Heron may offer a practical model for getting past it and one that could apply well beyond email. Bringing order to the chaos With a safe data set in place, the team were able to build and test Cuckoo, the capability at the heart of Project Kestrel. Where Tiger Heron solves the data problem, Cuckoo takes on the scale problem. Within a controlled test environment, Cuckoo uses machine learning to read through large volumes of emails and group them into meaningful clusters based on their content. Instead of opening every message individually, a KIM professional can see their data organised into coherent groupings - similar topics, similar threads, similar types of content - presented through an interactive visual interface. That shift, from an undifferentiated pile to a structured view, changes what is possible. Reviewers can direct their attention where it matters most, spot patterns they might otherwise miss and make decisions that are easier to document and defend. Together, Tiger Heron and Cuckoo form an end-to-end prototype, generate realistic test data, then analyse it in a way that supports faster, more transparent decision-making. What careful experimentation looks like Phase 1 was never going to produce a finished product, and it was not designed to. Alongside the two tools, the team carried out user research with KIM professionals, gathered ethics input to ensure responsible practices were built in from the start, engaged stakeholders across government and developed best-practice materials to support what comes next. Human oversight has been central throughout; the goal is always to keep people in control of the decisions that matter. That is what responsible AI adoption actually looks like in practice, not bold claims about transformation, but careful groundwork, honest about what is working and what still needs testing. Project Kestrel is an early example of that kind of experimentation. The filing cabinet is still full. But there is now a better sense of how to approach it.

If you have a government use case where synthetic data could help you work around the challenges of personal data, get in touch with the AI and Data Readiness team on dataAIReadiness_incubator@dsit.gov.uk

description: Government email has been piling up for decades and sorting through it manually is no longer sustainable. Project Kestrel explores how AI and synthetic data could transform the way Knowledge and Information Management professionals work. Find out what responsible AI adoption looks like in practice.

title: Minister for Social Care writes to Councils to accelerate Motor Neurone Disease (MND) Care Access
authors: Iain MacBeath, Adult Social Care Delivery Senior Advisor, the Department of Health and Social Care

content.content: Following Baroness Casey’s recommendation in her Nuffield Trust speech in March this year, the Minister for Social Care has written to local authorities to encourage the fast-tracking of access to care for people with motor neurone disease (MND), ahead of wider reform.
Key extracts from the letter

"As you will know, Baroness Casey is chairing an independent commission into adult social care, reporting into the Prime Minister. Baroness Casey made a number of immediate recommendations in March this year, including a recommendation to fast track access to care and support for people with Motor Neurone Disease.

The Minister set out the immediate initial steps we are inviting local authorities to take to streamline and accelerate access to care and support for people with Motor Neurone Disease within existing frameworks, ahead of fuller collaborative reform.

Motor Neurone Disease is a severe, progressive and terminal condition that requires rapid, responsive care as needs quickly evolve. As part of her review, Baroness Casey heard directly from people with personal experience of Motor Neurone Disease about delays in accessing the right care and support, and the profound impact this can have on individuals and their families, including avoidable crises, hospital admissions, and a loss of independence and dignity…

… It is essential that services respond with pace, coordination and foresight to keep up with escalating and complex needs. The Department of Health and Social Care is already taking forward Baroness Casey’s recommendation at pace, working in partnership with the Motor Neurone Disease Association, as well as extensively across local government representatives, the NHS, wider sector partners, and drawing on the experiences of people with Motor Neurone Disease, to develop ways of driving both immediate improvements and more substantial reform.

In the meantime, there is immediate scope for many areas to better meet the needs of people with Motor Neurone Disease within existing frameworks and partnerships, including through prioritising timely, straightforward assessment processes and delivering coordinated, responsive care and support…
If you are not already doing so, I strongly encourage you to:

… Finally, while the letter focuses on Motor Neurone Disease as one of the most acute and time critical conditions, I would encourage you to consider how these approaches might also apply to people with similarly rapidly progressing needs."

title: Water and Wellbeing: The People And Nature Blue Spaces Report

content.content: By Fränze Kibowski, Senior Specialist - Social Sciences

This blog explains the results of the recent People and Nature Blue Spaces Report, discussing how we interact with places like beaches, rivers and lakes, while looking at how the findings will influence Natural England's work.
When was the last time you spent time outside near the sea, or a river?

Spending time in ‘blue spaces’ - places where water is a key part of the environment, such as rivers, lakes, canals, beaches and the coast – can have positive effects on our mental and physical wellbeing.
A new report from Natural England and NatCen explores how people use these spaces, what they value about them and what can make it easier for more people to visit.
Blue spaces are important to many people

The research found that almost half of adults in England (47%) visited a blue space in the previous month, highlighting the important role these places play in people’s lives and their connection with nature.
Participants consistently described blue spaces as calming and restorative. Many described visiting rivers, lakes and the coast when they wanted time to relax, reflect or cope with stress.
Blue spaces support a wide range of activities and experiences, from everyday walks and  exercise to socialising with family and friends, sightseeing, wildlife watching and connecting to nature.
Making blue spaces accessible for everyone
While many people enjoy blue spaces, the research found that opportunities to visit are not experienced equally across the population.

At Natural England, our ambition is for access to nature to be a normal part of everyday life for everyone. This research helps us better understand the barriers some people face in visiting blue spaces and identifies opportunities to make these valuable natural environments more accessible, welcoming and inclusive.

A range of factors can influence how often people visit, including access to transport (in particular a car), proximity to blue spaces, health considerations and wider socio-economic circumstances. Because many blue spaces are destinations people travel to rather than places encountered during everyday routines, transport and accessibility can play an even more important role than with green spaces.
Quality matters
The condition of blue spaces was another important theme throughout the research.

Litter, pollution, poor maintenance and concerns about water quality can discourage people from spending time there. Safety was also important, particularly in winter when reduced daylight can make some places feel less accessible.
People said they would be more likely to use blue spaces if they were clean, well maintained, easy to access and felt safe throughout the year.
Supporting greater engagement

The findings from the country-wide  Adults’ People and Nature Survey and more in-depth focus groups both show that blue spaces have an important role to play alongside green spaces. By improving access and quality, more people can experience the health, wellbeing and nature benefits that these environments provide.

This report highlights several ways to help more people benefit from blue spaces. These include improving accessibility and transport links, investing in maintenance and environmental quality, and addressing barriers faced by groups who currently visit less often.

This summer, Natural England will be sharing affordable ideas and inspiration to help people access and enjoy local green and blue spaces. Whether it’s exploring a stretch of the King Charles III England Coast Path, taking a walk along a local river, so spending time beside a canal or lake, there are plenty of opportunities to enjoy the benefits of blue spaces.

Wherever you choose to visit, please help protect these special places by following the Countryside Code and, if you're heading out on the water or to the coast, the Paddlers' Code and Marine and Coastal Wildlife Code, helping us all to Respect, Protect and Enjoy our blue spaces.
The full report and a summary report can be found here.

title: SFI26: an update

content.content: It's encouraging to see so many farmers engaging with the Sustainable Farming Incentive 2026 (SFI26) since Window 1 opened in June.
Window 1 was designed to give smaller farms and those not already receiving ELM revenue funding an early opportunity to access the scheme.
It formed part of our plans to make funding simpler, fairer and more accessible to a wider range of farm businesses.
Uptake of SFI26 agreements in Window 1 so far
The Rural Payments Agency (RPA) began making SFI26 agreement offers to Window 1 applicants in July.
We’re pleased that, of the 1,188 agreements offered to farmers so far, 922 were accepted by 31 July. This meant they were able to start on 1 August.
To date, around two-thirds of farmers have accepted their agreement offer within 2 days.
The RPA continues to make agreement offers. We encourage farmers to accept their offers as quickly as possible.
Sites of Special Scientific Interest (SSSIs)
If you’ve applied for SFI26 on SSSI land, it’s important that you submit the required SSSI notice to get consent from Natural England as soon as possible.
The RPA cannot offer you an SFI26 agreement until you’ve done this. Read section 10.1 ‘SSSI consent’ in the SFI26 scheme rules and guidance to find out how to do this.
Budget allocation and the closure of Window 1
The available budget for Window 1 is £60 million. We’ve published budget updates on the blog, based on SFI26 applications received so far.
We said that Window 1 was expected to remain open for around 2 months, unless all the available funding for this window was allocated sooner.
This means Window 1 will close no later than 11:59pm on 28 August 2026.
Eligible farmers for Window 1 who do not apply during this window can apply in Window 2 instead.
Applying in Window 2
Window 2 will open in September 2026 for all farmers and land managers.
We’ll confirm the date we expect to open applications once Window 1 has closed.
The available budget for Window 2 will be £180 million. Any funding not allocated through Window 1 will be added to the budget for Window 2.
Starting an application for Window 2 early
Farmers whose ELM revenue agreements were due to expire would normally have to wait until those agreements ended before being able to apply for a new agreement.

As we confirmed in our blog post on 30 June, we will introduce a new feature in the SFI26 application service for farmers with eligible ELM revenue agreements that expire by the end of February 2027 to start an application early.
This means they can begin an SFI26 application and apply for land that is currently in their ELM revenue agreement before that agreement ends.
This will take effect when Window 2 opens. We will test and refine the new feature in the application service with a small number of farmers and land managers before it is available to everyone.
We've published additional information in the SFI26 scheme rules and guidance on GOV.UK explaining how this will work. Read section 3.8 ‘If your ELM revenue agreement is ending soon (Window 2 only)’.
Make sure you’re ready to apply
Before you start an SFI26 application for Window 1 or Window 2, read the ‘Get ready to apply’ guidance in the SFI26 scheme rules and guidance.
It explains the steps you need to take before you start your application, so the process is as straightforward as possible.

This includes making sure that the land parcels you want to include in your application are shown correctly on your digital maps. If these land details are not correct, it may prevent you from applying for SFI26.
Learn more
SFI26 scheme information
The SFI26 scheme information published on GOV.UK includes:
SFI: Getting started leaflet
We’ve put together a leaflet to help you understand the Sustainable Farming Incentive and how to get started – download it.
SFI: planning your fertiliser and nutrient use
This leaflet sets out the SFI actions that can help improve nutrient use efficiency and reduce reliance on fossil fuel-based fertilisers, supporting more sustainable and resilient farming practices.
Subscribe to the Farming Blog
For the latest updates from the Farming and Countryside team, subscribe to the Farming Blog.
By subscribing, you’ll receive an email whenever a new post is published.
