title: Turning ambition into action in complex systems

content.content: Turning ambition into outcomes is hard. We often know what "good" looks like, but the challenge for government is translating that vision into action quickly, efficiently and at scale for citizens.

A clear direction is essential for making good delivery decisions, but you can’t wait for a perfect picture of the end state before you act. That’s the CustomerFirst approach: start early, test, learn and adapt. The priority is turning ambition into thousands of decisions, trade-offs and improvements across a complex system as quickly as possible and learning from the results.
HMLR transformation

HM Land Registry (HMLR) has a critical role in maintaining the definitive land register of England and Wales, covering £9 trillion of property. HMLR has a vision for simpler services for citizens – designed around life events – which a NewCo approach might help translate into fast, tangible progress.

To get started, over the past two months, we have looked at the service that enables you to update the land register when a co-owner of a property dies – the Deceased Joint Proprietor service. If you’ve used it, you’ll know it's a relatively simple administrative task that still requires a paper-based form, with accompanying guidance that users struggle to follow, often at a very difficult time in their lives. Many of the 21,500 citizens who apply each year end up phoning the call centre for advice or submitting applications with errors.

We tested an alternative service model on a small, controlled sample of citizens. An online form, with overhauled and simplified guidance, and a built-in triage system that made it easier and quicker for people to apply. It's an initial, positive step in the right direction that built momentum for further change, as we seek to translate our ambition into delivery.

It also showed what a fast design sprint could achieve. We deliberately avoided over-designing the vision, plans or solution and focused on what we could improve right now. Testing allowed us to collaborate, learn about each organisation, and build an evidence base, rather than relying on assumptions, to shape what comes next.
Lessons for success
CustomerFirst has been in operation since January 2026 and we have learnt a lot about what helps NewCo projects emerge, and the balance between vision and action.
Keeping the momentum going

HMLR is building on these early foundations and applying these lessons, by broadening their NewCo approach to a set of experiments covering several existing citizen service areas. They are working to fully transform the Deceased Joint Proprietor service with a test and learn approach, as well as cracking cross-cutting challenges like improved identity verification and assurance and integrating further with other government services.

The experience of HMLR shows that starting small, learning fast and building evidence early can create momentum for much bigger change, and drive conversations about the end state. Every improvement teaches us something about users, services and the barriers to progress. Over time, those lessons become the foundation for transforming entire systems.
The biggest risk in transformation can be waiting for certainty before taking action.

description: Transforming complex public services starts with action, not perfection. Learn how HM Land Registry used rapid testing, evidence and collaboration to improve a citizen service and build momentum for wider change.

title: Explore More for Less: Affordable West Midlands Nature Escapes

content.content: This summer, if you’re looking for fun and accessible days out that are low-cost, then we have you covered. Not only is spending time in nature great for your wellbeing, it can also be great for your bank balance. Here are our suggestions for our favourite affordable days out in the West Midlands!

Summer is here, and the West Midlands is home to some of England's best-kept secrets when it comes to affordable, accessible nature. Whether you're after dramatic upland views, ancient woodland, or a wetland reserve buzzing with wildlife, there's something here for every family, every budget, and every level of mobility.
We've picked out five brilliant places to explore this summer, all either free to enter or costing very little, and all reachable without a car if you plan ahead.
Cheltenham Escarpment National Nature Reserve (NNR), Gloucestershire

Better known locally as Leckhampton Hill and Charlton Kings Common, this is one of England's newest NNRs, designated in June 2026, and home to the legendary 'Devil's Chimney'. This striking limestone pillar is thought to have been left standing by quarry workers. Although local folklore insists it was built by the Devil himself, so he'd have somewhere to sit and throw stones at churchgoers below. Who are we to say? But we do know the site contains the thickest inland sequences of Jurassic limestone and supports nationally important limestone grassland, home to wildflowers and 33 recorded butterfly species including the rare Duke of Burgundy.

The hill has panoramic views over Cheltenham, the Severn Vale and the Welsh hills and is part of the King's Series of National Nature Reserves, created to mark the Coronation of His Majesty King Charles III. Entry is free, and there are paths and tracks that the whole family can explore, including a 3km walk suitable for pushchairs and wheelchair users.
Getting there: There are four car parks on site, at Daisy Bank Road and Hartley Lane. The hill is a short distance from Cheltenham town centre and well served by local buses.
Sutton Park National Nature Reserve (NNR), Birmingham

One of the largest urban parks in Europe, Sutton Park is a 2,100-acre National Nature Reserve just six miles from Birmingham city centre, and it's completely free to visit. Inside you'll find heathland, woodland, seven lakes, and even grazing cattle and wild ponies. There's a 5-kilometre walking route and two playgrounds, making it ideal for younger children. The visitor centre has toilets, baby changing facilities and maps to help you find your way.

The park forms part of Purple Horizons, a Natural England-led nature recovery project working to connect Sutton Park with Cannock Chase, creating a wildlife corridor across the West Midlands urban fringe.

Getting there: The Town Gate entrance is a seven-minute walk from Sutton Coldfield train station, which is accessible via a twenty-minute train from Birmingham New Street. Buses 6, 935, 937, X3 and X5 also stop nearby.
Hall Green Naturehood Trail, Birmingham (National Trust and Go Jauntly)

For an option even closer to Birmingham city centre, try the Hall Green Naturehood Trail, a free 4.7km circular walk created by the National Trust in partnership with the Go Jauntly app. The route links green and blue spaces across Hall Green, starting at the historic Sarehole Mill, one of Birmingham's last two working watermills.

Along the way you'll pass the River Cole, wildflower meadows, and Trittiford Mill Pool, home to swans, ducks and dragonflies. The trail includes fun prompts for families, from birdwatching tips to "cloud-spotting." Download the free app for step-by-step directions or print the PDF guide in advance.
Getting there: The walk starts at Sarehole Mill, with a bus stop directly outside served by routes 5 and 11C Outer Circle.
Brandon Marsh Nature Reserve, Coventry (Warwickshire Wildlife Trust Wildlife Trust)
Brandon Marsh is a Warwickshire Wildlife Trust Wildlife Trust reserve known for its pools, reedbeds and woodland, and home to kingfishers, otters and muntjac deer.

Two surfaced trails, the Kingfisher Trail and the Woodpecker Trail, make this a great choice for buggies, wheelchairs and mobility scooters, and the reserve even offers free mobility scooter loans if you call ahead. Nine bird hides give you the chance to get up close to the wildlife, and the visitor centre has a café, shop and picnic area to round off your visit.
Entry costs £4.75 for adults, with concessions and family tickets available, and it's free for Wildlife Trust members.
Getting there: Brandon Marsh is on Brandon Lane, Coventry, with an on-site car park. Bike parking is also available.
Stiperstones Landscape National Nature Reserve (NNR), Shropshire

Stiperstones covers 1,562 hectares of dramatic upland heath, ancient woodland and rare geology along the Shropshire Hills. It's part of the King's Series and is managed by a partnership including Natural England, Forestry England, Shropshire Wildlife Trust and local community groups.

Entry is free. Start at the NNR car park, where you'll find a 650-metre all-ability trail alongside longer walking routes if you fancy tackling the full ridge. Keep an eye out for the legendary Devil's Chair, a rock formation shattered by ice-age freezing that has inspired ghost stories for centuries, and look out for red grouse, emperor moths and the increasingly rare bilberry bumblebee along the way.

If you'd rather leave the car at home, the Shropshire Hills Shuttle Bus runs every weekend from May to September, taking in the Long Mynd, Carding Mill Valley and Stiperstones itself, with adult tickets from £2 and free travel for under-16s. It's a brilliant, low-cost way to see some of Shropshire's best scenery without worrying about parking.

Getting there: The reserve is 3km east of the A488, with car parking available at the main NNR car park, the Bog, and Snailbeach. Alternatively, catch the Shropshire Hills Shuttle Bus from Church Stretton.
A couple more favourites

Chapter Meadows Nature Reserve in Worcester sits alongside the River Severn, just a mile from Worcester Foregate Street train station. Painswick Beacon in Gloucestershire is the site of an Iron Age hillfort, standing 283 metres high with some of the best 360-degree views in the Cotswolds. Painswick Beacon is on a bus route, and you can download the Gloucestershire Walks app for a map to guide you.

Or for some options even closer to home Local Nature Reserves are places valued for their wildlife or geology, designated by local councils for people to enjoy and learn from. Find your nearest one: Local Nature Reserves (England) | Natural England Open Data Geoportal

With the recent dry, hot weather, wildfire risk is high across the countryside. Please pack a picnic instead of a barbecue, take your rubbish home with you, and if you spot an unattended fire, get to a safe place and call 999.
Remember to always follow the Countryside Code when you’re out and about in nature!

The Countryside Code is a simple guide to helping everyone enjoy the outdoors responsibly while protecting the natural environment. It encourages visitors to respect other people, protect plants, animals and habitats, and leave gates, paths and property as they find them. By following the Countryside Code, we can all play our part in keeping nature accessible, safe and enjoyable for everyone, while helping to conserve the landscapes and wildlife that make our countryside so special.

title: Tackling digital exclusion through community connections

title: How collaboration underpins our annual ICT sustainability report

content.content: Anna Fountain explains why the input of so many contributors from across departments is so fundamental to producing the Government’s annual health check of ICT sustainability.

If you've ever wrestled with spreadsheets, chased down asset numbers, questioned whether a device should sit in one category or another, or spent time tracking down supplier data, then you may have contributed to this year’s Greening Government ICT Annual Report 2024–25.

The publication of the annual report marks another important milestone in government's journey towards more sustainable digital and technology services. Behind every figure in the report is a huge amount of work from colleagues across government who collect, validate and submit the data that makes reporting possible.
So, before we continue, we'd like to start a thank you to those colleagues who contributed.

One of the things that makes the Greening Government ICT reporting process unique is the scale of collaboration involved. Teams from across government, including sustainability specialists, asset managers and suppliers all play a part in helping us understand the environmental impact of government ICT.

The annual report provides an important evidence base for understanding where we're making progress and where further work is needed and data gaps remain. But it can only do that because colleagues across government invest the time to gather the underlying information.

Whilst there are still significant improvements to be made, the quality of our reporting continues to improve year on year, giving us greater confidence in the data and better insight into the environmental impact of our technology estates across hosting and hardware.
Progress on digital sustainability performance

This report covers the digital sustainability performance of every UK Government department over the 2024–25 financial year and highlights the impact UK Government’s IT estate has. For example, we generated nearly 300,000 tonnes of CO2 emissions in 2024-5. Similarly, UK Government was responsible for over 950 tonnes of IT waste (and has over 900,00 laptops in its estate). This shows we have a big opportunity to embed circularity and minimise waste, delivering cost savings & using taxpayer money responsibly.

It’s encouraging that the report shows that emissions and e-waste from UK Government’s IT estate reduced in 2024-5, and that we continued to meet our target of sending less than 1% of e-waste to landfill. The progress shown in this report should give us confidence to continue innovating and working across departments and supply chains to deliver a more sustainable IT estate for UK Government
Sustainability isn't just a reporting exercise

It's easy to see the annual return as a once-a-year activity, but the report demonstrates something much broader: sustainability is increasingly becoming part of how government designs, delivers and manages digital services.
Every decision matters.

Whether it's extending the life of an end-user device, consolidating infrastructure, embedding GreenOps into cloud design, or ensuring equipment is reused before recycling, small actions taken across thousands of assets can have a significant impact.

The report shows that departments continue to make progress while managing growing demand for digital services and technology. As government becomes increasingly digital, continuing to understand and manage the environmental impact of ICT will remain essential.
Improving the numbers behind the numbers
This year's report also reflects continued improvements in the way we estimate and report emissions and energy consumption.

We would like to acknowledge the contribution of GDSA members, Ewen Anderson, Anthony Levy & Mark Butcher, who have provided invaluable support in improving our underlying estimations of Scope 3 embodied carbon and energy consumption calculations. These are complex areas where data availability and methodology continue to evolve, and the expertise shared across the community has played an important role in helping improve the quality and consistency of reporting.
A growing sustainability community
One of the most encouraging aspects of recent years has been the growth of the digital sustainability community across government and the public sector.

What started as a relatively small group of specialists has developed into a network of practitioners who are actively sharing ideas, lessons learned and good practice. Through forums such as the GDSA, colleagues are helping one another tackle common challenges, improve data quality and identify opportunities to reduce environmental impact.
That collaboration is essential. No single team or organisation has all the answers, but together we are building a stronger evidence base and a more mature approach to sustainable ICT.
Looking ahead
The insights contained within the report helps shape our strategy and guides individual departments understand the environmental impacts associated with their ICT estates.
We have been working across government and with industry and academia to develop a new UK Government Digital Sustainability Strategy to set out our priorities over the next few years to deliver:

The publication of the annual report is not the end of the process, it's an opportunity to learn, improve and build momentum. By using these insights to inform decision-making, drive collaboration and identify opportunities for improvement, we can continue to deliver meaningful change and ensure that government ICT supports environmental objectives, wider economic and social outcomes, and the efficient use of taxpayers’ money through more sustainable, resilient and cost-effective digital services.

title: Apply now for automation and robotics funding

content.content: Round 2 of the Farming Futures Automation and Robotics competition is now open for applications.

The £20 million competition is part of the Farming Innovation Programme. It supports collaborative projects developing practical automation and robotics technologies that help farmers, growers and foresters improve productivity, manage labour pressures and make everyday tasks more efficient.

Funding is available for innovative tools and systems that address real-world challenges across agriculture, horticulture and forestry in England, including activities such as planting, crop management and harvesting.
The competition is designed to bring together researchers, businesses and industry partners to develop solutions with clear commercial potential and practical on-farm benefits.

This round is open to a broader range of sectors than the 2023 competition. It includes ornamental plant propagation, growing and monitoring, where technologies could also have applications in food-producing horticulture.

Eligible forestry projects include tree nursery and planting operations, woodland monitoring and woodland management systems. Projects focused on heavy machinery and harvesting operations are not eligible.
Apply now
Projects must be collaborative, have a total value of between £500,000 and £2.5 million, and demonstrate how they will address industry challenges and support sustainable growth.
Full details, including eligibility criteria, application guidance and how to apply, are available through the Innovation Funding Service.
The deadline to apply is 30 September 2026 at 11am.
Join our webinars
If you’d like to learn more about the competition and how to apply, Innovate UK will host a series of webinars this month.
Briefing for applicants

This webinar will provide information about the aims, scope and content of the competition. The team will provide details of the application process, eligibility, assessment processes and what support is available for applicants. There will also be a Q&A session where you can put your questions to the team.
This webinar will take place 6 August at 2pm.
Joining link
Consortia building

This webinar will cover the content and aims of the competition including consortium building advice and networking. During the event, you can meet others interested in the competition and explore potential collaborations. There will also be a Q&A session where you can put your questions to the team.
This webinar will take place 13 August at 10am.
Register to attend.
If you can't attend any of these sessions, you will be able to access the recordings on our webinars page.
Case studies: automation in farming
Automation and robotics have the potential to effectively respond to real farm needs.
Vineyard Information System for Technology and Automation (VISTA)
In 2023, we awarded £786,220 to fund a project developing an open-source digital mapping platform for vineyards to support data-driven and autonomous farming.
Outfield Technologies Ltd are leading on this, alongside the UK Agri-Tech Centre, JoJo’s Vineyard, Antobot, the University of Lincoln and Vinescapes.
The Vineyard Information System for Technology and Automation (VISTA) project is developing high-resolution vineyard maps using drone and robotic technology.

Designed with growers and agri-tech companies in mind, these maps will help to speed up adoption of automation. The maps are easy to integrate with existing farming systems and support a shift to more data-driven activities.

One application of the technology is improving harvest planning. By generating highly accurate yield estimates, growers can make better informed decisions, secure the best prices for their crops and reduce the amount of crop waste.

The maps also support precision growing by creating maps for GPS-guided machinery which allow chemicals or fertilisers to be applied in varying rates. This will help to reduce the amount of chemicals used and could improve crop yields.
The project aims to help vineyard growers in England improve productivity, profitability and sustainability, while creating systems that could be adopted internationally.
Agaricus Robotic Harvester
Led by Agaricus Robotics alongside Littleport Mushrooms and the University of Lincoln, this  project was awarded £772,425 in funding in 2023.
The team developed the world's first robotic mushroom harvesting system used in a commercial setting.

They built a highly accurate robotic harvester that scans the mushroom bed prior to picking and uses a soft gripper to pick the mushrooms with minimal damage. It measures and trims the mushroom stalks to the desired length as specified by the farm, minimising farm waste.

The technology aims to increase productivity, reduce labour shortages and production costs. It also has the potential to cut food waste and strengthen the UK's leadership in the world of advanced agricultural robotics.

You can connect with others interested in this competition by joining the Innovate UK Farming Innovation Programme LinkedIn group.

title: Building Defra’s software development profession for the AI age

content.content: Principal Software Developer John Watson shares how he and his colleagues are exploring how they can use AI to drive efficiencies.

It is an exciting time to be a software developer. Artificial intelligence (AI) is helping us explore ideas, understand complex systems, reduce repetitive work and turn concepts into working software faster.

The technology is also moving beyond tools that suggest code or answer questions. Agentic AI can plan work, explore codebases and carry out multi-step tasks. Used well, it gives developers more time to solve difficult problems and improve public services. Using AI badly can spread misinformation, invade privacy, reinforce bias, weaken human skills, create security risks, and harm environmental sustainability.

Across Defra, developers are approaching these opportunities with curiosity and energy. As Principal developers, we want to build on that by giving people the skills, guidance and confidence to experiment responsibly and securely.

That momentum is visible in our usage data. Since October 2025, active users in the software development profession have increased 11-fold. Over the same period, chat and agent interactions rose from 780 to more than 10,000 interactions a month, showing growth in both breadth and depth of adoption.
Building skills around developers’ needs
Developers are at different stages in their use of AI. Some already use effective agentic workflows; others are still building confidence and learning where the tools add value.

To support that range of experience, we have invested in GitHub Copilot and worked with Microsoft to provide remote and on-site learning. The wider offer includes self-paced courses, practical workshops and opportunities to work towards certification.

The figures suggest this investment is translating into sustained use. Monthly active users rose steadily through the first half of 2026, while engaged users stayed consistently high. In most months, 85% to 96% of active users did more than open the tool: they used a suggestion, showing practical value rather than one-off experimentation.
Learning from each other
Several developers who attended the Microsoft sessions then organised local knowledge-sharing events to help colleagues apply AI to their own work.

This peer-led learning matters because useful techniques are often grounded in a specific service, codebase or delivery challenge. Seeing a colleague use plan mode, custom instructions or an agentic workflow in practice can be more valuable than discussing the technology in the abstract.
Our community of practice helps keep that conversation going, giving colleagues a place to share experiences and exchange ideas across teams.

We have also built a strong two-way relationship with Defra’s AI capability and enablement team. They provide opportunities to trial emerging tools, while developers share evidence to support wider learning.

For junior developers, AI is also becoming a useful learning mentor, helping them explore unfamiliar concepts and ask questions as they work. It’s important for me to emphasise that this positively augments, rather than replaces, mentoring, pairing and support from experienced colleagues.
Three of our developers also took part in a cross-government AI hackathon, finishing third ahead of more than 30 other teams.
Using evidence to guide responsible adoption

To guide this work, we surveyed developers to understand how AI tools are used across teams, roles and technology stacks. We invited views from everyone, including those who were enthusiastic, cautious or sceptical, so our strategy reflects the profession’s collective needs.

We are also looking at utilisation data alongside survey responses. Interactions grew faster than active users: around 13 times higher from October to June, compared with an 11-fold increase in active users. This shows the conversation is not just about more people trying AI, but about developers using it more deeply in day-to-day workflows.

The responses showed where developers find AI most useful across the software development lifecycle, which tools and models suit different tasks, and where knowledge gaps remain. They also highlighted concerns about sustainability, wellbeing and using AI without enough planning or oversight.

We are using that evidence to shape our learning offer and refine our software development standards and guidance. From a sustainability perspective, this includes encouraging developers to plan before asking AI to act, choose a suitable model for the task, and create reusable instructions, skills and custom agents to reduce  ‘ping-pong’ conversations, unnecessary credit use and energy consumption.
We have published a GitHub Copilot guide to support developers in adopting the technology, with sustainability notes explicitly highlighted.
Looking ahead
Looking ahead, we will continue to shape AI use across the profession through evidence, not assumption, focusing on where it can help Defra deliver its goals.
Our education offer will keep evolving, with sustainable AI use built in as we continue to look for efficiency gains.
We are excited about the opportunities ahead and confident that evidence-based decisions will help Defra make the most of AI across digital delivery.

title: Digital resilience - a priority for pensions

content.content: In a world where digital systems underpin nearly every aspect of our lives, the pensions industry is no exception.
Pension schemes today are powered by a web of interconnected technology and with that comes growing risk.
Digital resilience is an organisation’s ability to prepare for, respond to, and recover from IT disruptions—whether it’s a cyber-attack, data breach, system outage or even a simple human error.
It includes cybersecurity, but also covers non-malicious disruption such as outages, supplier failures and errors. Recent cyber-attacks have made the risk all too clear.

In the last few years, a number of high-profile UK organisations have suffered serious cyber incidents that compromised online and personal data, affecting millions of individuals – this includes pension administrators. These incidents are not isolated: they highlight a broader trend. Cyber threats are escalating, and pension schemes can be in the firing line.
Why does digital resilience matter for pensions?

For the pensions industry, the stakes are high. Pension schemes hold sensitive personal and financial data. They serve millions of members who depend on timely payments. A single digital failure can have serious consequences, shake confidence, delay payments and put members’ personal information at risk.
Digital resilience helps prevent this from happening. It's about making sure the systems you rely on every day don’t let administrators or members down.
What's at stake?
Pension schemes can be attractive targets.

Hackers know that pension systems store sensitive data, from National Insurance numbers to bank details and addresses. With millions of items of members’ personal and financial information under one digital roof, the potential reward for cybercriminals is large.

But it does not stop there. Many pension schemes are connected to multiple third-party suppliers from software providers to payroll processors. These external connections can inadvertently create a potential “back door” into systems. If just one supplier has weak security, it can be exploited to access the broader ecosystem, putting pension schemes and members at risk.
And it's not just about hackers. A failed software update, a server outage or a simple case of human error can be just as damaging.
In a highly regulated industry built on trust, even short-term disruption can have long-term consequences. That's why digital resilience is essential.
The regulatory push

The Pensions Regulator (TPR) has placed digital resilience high on the agenda, urging schemes to modernise data management, tighten up digital defences, and take operational resilience seriously. Digital resilience is not just a “nice to have,” but a critical part of scheme governance.
What can schemes do?
The good news is, you do not have to be a cybersecurity expert to enhance scheme digital resilience.
With the right mindset and a few practical steps, pension schemes can significantly reduce their risk and be better prepared if something goes wrong.
Here are 5 key actions every pension scheme should consider:

Get the basics right: strong passwords, multi-factor authentication, encryption, regular software updates. These may sound basic but they are the first line of defence. Go a step further with real-time monitoring tools to detect suspicious activity and regular penetration testing to identify vulnerabilities before attackers do. Work closely with administrators and third-party suppliers to ensure security protocols are aligned across the board.
It's not just about preventing problems - it is about responding to them effectively.

Develop clear incident response and disaster recovery plans. If your administration platform goes offline or is breached, you need to act fast. What is your plan B? How quickly can you recover? What is the process? Who needs to be involved? It needs to be safe, quick and transparent, minimising disruption and maintaining trust with members and regulators.

Your third-party providers, from software platforms to outsourced administrators, are part of your digital ecosystem. Carry out due diligence on suppliers’ security and resilience, including incident response, backup arrangements and recovery time objectives.

Technology alone is not enough, people matter too. Even the best systems can be undone by a well-meaning click on a phishing email. Human error is one of the biggest cybersecurity risks. Ensure everyone involved with the pension scheme receives regular training on digital threats, data handling and what to do when something does not look right.
Do not wait for a real crisis. Test your response and continuity plans regularly using real-world scenarios. Resilience is not theoretical, it's practical.
What you can do
No matter your role, you play a part in protecting members and their data. Here’s how you can help:
Final thoughts
Digital resilience is not just a technology issue, it's a core part of running a secure, reliable and trusted pension scheme.

Whether you are a trustee, administrator or stakeholder or involved in scheme governance, the risks are real, but so are the opportunities to build smarter, safer and more future-proof operations. In today’s digital world, digital resilience isn’t optional. It's essential.
